title: The first five minutes
prompt: The interviewer says "Design a photo-sharing app." What do you do before drawing any boxes?
explanation: Pin down the scope: list 3–4 core features (functional requirements) and the qualities that matter (scale, latency, consistency, availability). A rough estimate of users and read/write ratio decides whether you need caching, sharding or queues at all. Jumping straight into components is the most common way candidates fail.
hint: Two kinds of requirements, then a number or two.

title: What CAP actually says
prompt: Which statement about the CAP theorem is accurate?
choices: Pick any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance
When the network splits, a replica must either refuse requests (stay consistent) or answer with possibly stale data (stay available)
SQL databases are CA and NoSQL databases are AP
The C in CAP means the same thing as the C in ACID
explanation: Partitions happen in any distributed system, so P isn't optional. The real choice is C or A during a partition. "Pick two" is the popular but misleading version. Database labels like "CA" don't hold up either: a single-node database isn't distributed, and many databases let you tune the trade-off. CAP's C means every read sees the latest write (linearizability). ACID's C means the data obeys your constraints. Bonus: PACELC adds that else, with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency.
hint: Can a distributed system opt out of network failures?

title: Where eventual consistency is fine
prompt: In a marketplace app, which feature can safely be eventually consistent?
choices: Deducting money from a wallet balance
Reserving the last seat on a flight
The like count shown on a listing
Checking whether a username is already taken
explanation: If a like count is a few seconds behind, nobody is harmed. Money, the last unit of inventory and uniqueness checks all break if two replicas disagree: you get overdrafts, double bookings and duplicate usernames. Strong consistency costs latency and availability, so spend it only where a stale read causes real damage.
hint: Which one hurts nobody if it's a few seconds stale?

title: Database for orders and payments
prompt: An e-commerce app stores users, orders, line items and payments. Reports join across all of them. Which database fits best?
choices: A relational database such as PostgreSQL
A document store such as MongoDB, one document per user
A wide-column store such as Cassandra
A key-value store such as Redis
explanation: The data is relational, needs multi-row transactions (charge the card and create the order) and gets queried in ways you can't fully predict. That's what SQL is for, and Postgres scales further than most interviews require. Documents get awkward once you join across entities. Cassandra is built for huge write volume with known query patterns. Redis is a cache, not a system of record. Default to SQL and justify any move away from it.
hint: Joins plus transactions that touch several tables.

title: Storing billions of chat messages
prompt: A chat app writes billions of messages a day. Almost every read is "the latest 50 messages in conversation X". Which storage fits best?
choices: One big Postgres table with an index on created_at
Elasticsearch
A graph database
A wide-column store such as Cassandra, partitioned by conversation and sorted by time
explanation: Wide-column stores are built for huge append-heavy write volume and one known access pattern. Partition by conversation_id, sort by time, and "latest 50" becomes a single sequential read. One Postgres table hits write and size limits at this scale unless you shard it yourself. Elasticsearch suits searching messages, not storing them. A graph database solves a different problem: relationships between entities.
hint: Huge write volume, and a single query pattern you know in advance.

title: What Redis is good for
prompt: Which job is the worst fit for Redis?
choices: A cache in front of a slow database query
Per-user rate-limit counters with a TTL
A leaderboard (sorted set)
The only copy of user account data
explanation: Redis keeps data in memory. It can persist to disk, but the defaults can lose recent writes, and memory caps the size of the dataset. It shines for fast, rebuildable or short-lived data: caches, sessions, counters with expiry, sorted-set leaderboards and pub/sub. Keep your source of truth in a durable database.
hint: Where does Redis keep the data, and what happens on a crash?

title: Product search
prompt: Users need typo-tolerant, relevance-ranked search across 50M product listings. What's the usual approach?
choices: WHERE title LIKE '%term%' in the main database
A search index such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, kept in sync from the main database
Load every listing into the browser and filter on the client
A B-tree index on title
explanation: Search engines build an inverted index (term → documents) with fuzzy matching and ranking. Sync it from your database, for example via change-data-capture or a queue, and accept that results may lag by a few seconds. A leading-wildcard LIKE can't use a B-tree index, so it scans every row. A B-tree helps only with prefix matches, never with typos or ranking.
hint: Think of the index at the back of a book.

title: Where uploaded images go
prompt: Users upload profile photos and videos. Where should the files live?
choices: As BLOBs in the main SQL database
On the app server's local disk
In object storage (such as S3) served through a CDN, with only the URL or key in the database
Base64-encoded inside a JSON column
explanation: Object storage is cheap, durable and effectively unlimited, and a CDN serves the files from near the user. A common full-stack trick: the server hands the client a short-lived presigned URL, and the browser uploads straight to storage without tying up your servers. BLOBs bloat the database and its backups. A local disk disappears when you add a second server or replace this one. Base64 adds about 33% to the size.
hint: Your app servers should stay stateless, and the database should hold metadata.

title: Analytics dashboards
prompt: Product wants dashboards like "daily active users by country over 12 months", built from billions of events. Where should those queries run?
choices: On the production Postgres primary
In a columnar data warehouse (such as BigQuery, Snowflake or ClickHouse), loaded from events
In Redis
Computed in the browser from raw events
explanation: This is OLAP: scans and aggregates over a few columns of huge tables. Columnar stores read only the columns a query needs and compress them well. Running these queries on the transactional (OLTP) primary competes with user traffic and can slow the whole app. Redis and the browser can't hold billions of events.
hint: Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage.

title: Two buyers, one item left
prompt: Two requests both read stock = 1, both pass the check in app code and both write stock = 0. Two orders are created. What's the simplest correct fix?
choices: Add a cache in front of the stock read
Re-check the stock in the frontend before submitting
Run the check in a separate transaction before the write
Make the write conditional: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0, then check the affected row count
explanation: This is a lost update, a read-then-write race. A conditional update makes the database do the check and the write atomically, and the losing request sees 0 rows affected. SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside one transaction also works. The other choices still read first and write later, so the race window stays open. Postgres's default isolation level (Read Committed) doesn't prevent this on its own.
hint: Move the check to where the write happens.

title: Composite index order
prompt: A table has an index on (user_id, created_at). Which query can not use it efficiently?
choices: WHERE user_id = 7
WHERE user_id = 7 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
explanation: A B-tree on (a, b) is sorted by a first, like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. Queries that filter on a, on a and b, or on a sorted by b can use it. Filtering on b alone means checking every a group (the "leftmost prefix" rule). Also remember that every index speeds up reads but slows down writes.
hint: Can you look up everyone named "Sam" in a phone book sorted by last name?

title: The slow feed endpoint
prompt: GET /feed loads 50 posts, then runs a separate query for each post's author. Locally it's fast. In production it takes 2 s. What's the problem?
choices: The N+1 query problem: 51 database round trips instead of 1–2
The posts table needs a bigger cache
JSON serialization is slow
The CDN isn't caching the endpoint
explanation: Each query costs a network round trip, which is tiny locally and adds up in production. Fetch the authors in one go: a JOIN, WHERE id IN (…), your ORM's eager loading, or a DataLoader in GraphQL resolvers. GraphQL is especially prone to N+1 because each field resolves on its own.
hint: Count the queries.

title: Why stateless app servers?
prompt: Why do designs insist that web/API servers be stateless, and where does the state go instead?
explanation: If any server can handle any request, you can add or remove servers freely behind a load balancer (horizontal scaling), and a crash loses nothing. State moves to shared stores: sessions in Redis or a signed cookie, files in object storage, data in the database. Vertical scaling (a bigger machine) is simpler but has a ceiling and is a single point of failure.
hint: What happens to a user's session when the load balancer sends them to a different server?

title: Live score updates
prompt: A sports page pushes score updates to the browser every few seconds. The client never sends anything back. What's the simplest good choice?
choices: WebSockets
Server-Sent Events (EventSource)
Polling every 100 ms
WebRTC
explanation: SSE is one-way, server to client, over plain HTTP. It reconnects automatically and works with ordinary proxies and auth. WebSockets are two-way and earn their extra complexity in chat or multiplayer. Fast polling wastes requests, and slow polling adds delay. WebRTC is for peer-to-peer media. Gotcha: under HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only about 6 connections per domain, so many SSE tabs can starve each other. HTTP/2 fixes this.
hint: Data flows in only one direction.

title: Chat across many servers
prompt: Chat users hold WebSocket connections spread across 20 servers. Alice is connected to server 3 and Bob to server 11. How does Alice's message reach Bob?
choices: The load balancer forwards it automatically
Make all clients connect to one server
Server 3 publishes it to a pub/sub layer (such as Redis pub/sub or Kafka), and the server holding Bob's connection pushes it to him
Bob's client polls server 3
explanation: Each server knows only its own connections, so you need a backplane: publish by conversation or user, and every server delivers to its local sockets. A presence or connection registry can say which server holds whom. The load balancer only routes new connections. One server can't hold everyone, and a client can't know which server to poll. Also plan for reconnects: when a server restarts, clients reconnect and fetch what they missed.
hint: The servers need a way to talk to each other.

title: Keeping the cache fresh
prompt: With a cache-aside setup (read: check the cache, fall back to the DB, fill the cache), what should a profile update do?
choices: Update the DB, then delete the cache key
Update the cache, then the DB
Update only the cache. The DB catches up later
Nothing. The TTL will expire it eventually
explanation: Write to the source of truth first, then invalidate, so the next read refills the cache from fresh data. Updating the cache first leaves wrong data cached if the DB write fails. Writing only to the cache makes the cache the source of truth. Relying only on the TTL serves stale data until it expires. Still set a TTL as a backstop, because a small race remains (a slow reader can put back a stale value).
hint: Write the source of truth, then invalidate rather than update.

title: The homepage key expires
prompt: A hot cache key expires, and 5,000 requests miss at once and all hit the database, which falls over. What's this called, and what helps?
choices: Cache penetration. Fix: a bigger cache
Split brain. Fix: more replicas
Hot partition. Fix: a new shard key
Cache stampede (thundering herd). Fix: let one request rebuild while the others wait or get stale data, and add jitter to TTLs
explanation: Coalesce the misses with a lock or single-flight so only one request recomputes, serve the stale value while it refreshes, and randomize TTLs so keys don't all expire together. Cache penetration is a different problem: repeated lookups for keys that don't exist. Split brain and hot partitions concern replication and sharding.
hint: Thousands of requests all trying to rebuild the same value.

title: Caching a built web app
prompt: A Vite build outputs index.html and app.3f9a2c.js. Which Cache-Control headers fit?
choices: Both: max-age=31536000
Both: no-store
HTML: no-cache. Hashed JS: max-age=31536000, immutable
HTML: max-age=31536000. JS: no-cache
explanation: A hashed filename changes whenever its content changes, so it can be cached forever. The HTML must stay fresh because it points at the current hashes. Gotcha: no-cache doesn't mean "don't cache". It means "store it, but revalidate (ETag/304) before using it". no-store is the one that forbids storing. Caching the HTML for a year strands users on an old deploy.
hint: Which file's name changes when its content changes?

title: My edit disappeared
prompt: Writes go to the primary and reads go to async read replicas. A user saves their bio, the page reloads and shows the old bio. Why, and what's a common fix?
choices: Replication lag. Fix: read-your-writes, routing that user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write
The browser cached the old page. Fix: a hard refresh
The write failed. Fix: retry
A deadlock. Fix: increase the lock timeout
explanation: Asynchronous replicas trail the primary by milliseconds to seconds. Read-your-writes consistency means routing a user's reads to the primary after their own write, or waiting until a replica has caught up. Updating the UI optimistically from the response also hides the lag. Replicas scale reads, but they don't help with write load.
hint: Where did the write go, and where did the read come from?

title: Picking a shard key
prompt: You're sharding a tweets table. Which shard key causes a hot partition?
choices: hash(tweet_id)
hash(user_id), accepting that a celebrity's shard may get busy
created_date, so all of today's writes go to one shard
hash(user_id, tweet_id)
explanation: Sharding by time sends every new write to the newest shard while the old ones sit idle. A good key spreads load evenly and matches your common queries. user_id keeps a user's tweets together but can make a celebrity's shard hot. A tweet-id hash spreads load evenly but makes "all tweets by a user" fan out to every shard. Shard only once replicas, caching and a bigger box are exhausted, because cross-shard joins and transactions get hard.
hint: Which key sends every new write to the same place?

title: When to add a queue
prompt: Signup must also send a welcome email, resize the avatar and sync to the CRM. Why put those behind a message queue, and what's the catch?
explanation: The request returns as soon as the user row is saved. Slow or flaky work runs in background workers that retry on failure and can scale on their own, and the queue absorbs traffic spikes. The catch: most queues deliver at least once, so each job must be idempotent (sending the email twice must be harmless), and the results are eventually consistent.
hint: Think about request latency, failure and spikes. Then: how many times can a message arrive?

title: Double charge on retry
prompt: The client sends POST /payments, the network times out and the client retries. The server had actually processed the first request, so the user is charged twice. What's the standard fix?
choices: Never retry POST requests
Make it a GET
The client generates an idempotency key per payment attempt and sends it with every retry. The server stores the result per key and returns that result for repeats
Increase the client timeout
explanation: A timeout doesn't tell the client whether the server did the work, so retries must be safe. With a stored key and a unique constraint, repeats return the original response instead of charging again. Stripe's API works this way. Never retrying gives up on transient failures. GET must not have side effects. A longer timeout only makes the race less likely.
hint: How can the server tell that two requests are the same attempt?

title: Rate limiting an API
prompt: You need to limit each API key to 100 requests per minute while allowing short bursts, across 10 API servers. What's a solid design?
choices: A counter in each server's memory
A token bucket per key in a shared store such as Redis. Over the limit, return 429 with Retry-After
Disable the client's button for 1 s after each click
Return 500 when traffic is high
explanation: A token bucket refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to its size. The state must be shared, or each of the 10 servers allows 100 and the real limit becomes 1,000. 429 Too Many Requests tells clients to back off, and Retry-After says for how long. Client-side throttling is nice UX, but it isn't enforcement. 500 tells clients the server broke.
hint: Where does the counter live if there are 10 servers?

title: Infinite scroll pagination
prompt: An infinite-scroll feed uses ?offset=…&limit=20. Users see duplicate posts as new ones arrive, and deep pages are slow. What's better?
choices: Bigger pages
Load the whole feed once
Page numbers instead of offsets
Cursor (keyset) pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
explanation: An offset counts rows, so new inserts shift everything and you see duplicates. OFFSET 10000 still reads and throws away 10,000 rows. A cursor remembers where you stopped, is stable under inserts, and is an index seek at any depth. Include a unique tiebreaker such as id, or rows with equal timestamps get skipped. Page numbers are just offsets. The trade-off: you can't jump to page 37.
hint: Remember a position, not a count.

title: When GraphQL earns its keep
prompt: Which is the strongest reason to choose GraphQL over REST?
choices: It's faster because it uses a binary protocol
Several clients (web, iOS, Android) need different shapes of deeply related data, and you want to avoid over-fetching and many round trips
It caches better at the CDN out of the box
It removes the need for authorization checks
explanation: GraphQL lets each client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one request. The costs: a single POST endpoint loses free HTTP/CDN caching, N+1 resolvers need DataLoader, and malicious deep queries need depth or cost limits. It's JSON over HTTP, not binary (that's gRPC), and you still authorize every field.
hint: Who benefits from choosing their own response shape?

title: Sessions vs JWTs
prompt: Which statement about JWT auth for a web app is accurate?
choices: A JWT can't be revoked before it expires unless you add server-side state, such as a denylist or short expiry with refresh tokens
JWTs are encrypted, so the payload is secret
localStorage is the safest place to keep them
JWTs make CSRF impossible no matter where they're stored
explanation: A JWT is self-contained, so the server trusts it until exp. That's why access tokens are short-lived (minutes) and paired with a revocable refresh token. A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone can base64-decode it. localStorage is readable by any XSS script, while an HttpOnly cookie isn't. A cookie brings CSRF back, though, so use SameSite or CSRF tokens. Plain server sessions are often the simpler choice for one web app.
hint: What does the server have to remember to log someone out?

title: Rendering strategy
prompt: Which pairing is the best fit?
choices: Marketing pages and blog → client-side render (CSR); logged-in analytics dashboard → static generation (SSG)
Everything → SSR on every request
Product pages that change hourly → static generation with periodic revalidation (ISR); logged-in dashboard → CSR or SSR
Everything → CSR, because SEO no longer matters
explanation: Public pages that need SEO and fast first paint suit pre-rendered or cached HTML (SSG/ISR), refreshed on a schedule or on demand. Private, highly personal screens gain nothing from SEO, so CSR or SSR is fine. CSR for marketing pages hurts first paint and crawlability, and SSG can't pre-render per-user data. SSR on every request costs server time on pages that could be cached.
hint: Ask two questions per page: does SEO matter, and how personal is the data?

title: Search-as-you-type
prompt: A search box fires a request on every keystroke. Results flicker, and older responses sometimes overwrite newer ones. Which set of fixes is right?
choices: Debounce input (~200–300 ms), cancel or ignore stale requests (AbortController or a request id), and cache results per query
Throttle to one request per 5 s
Fetch the whole dataset on page load
Add a loading spinner
explanation: Debouncing cuts the number of requests. Cancelling, or keeping only the latest response, fixes the race where a slow response for "re" lands after the one for "react". A small cache makes backspacing instant. The server side should be a prefix index (trie or search engine) with short TTL caching. A 5 s throttle feels broken, loading everything doesn't scale, and a spinner hides nothing.
hint: Two problems: too many requests, and responses arriving out of order.

title: Back-of-the-envelope QPS
prompt: 10 million daily active users each make about 20 API requests a day. Roughly what's the average request rate?
choices: ~200 req/s
explanation: 200M requests ÷ ~100,000 seconds per day (86,400, rounded) ≈ 2,000 req/s. Peaks are often 2–5× the average, so plan for about 5–10k. That's comfortably handled by a few stateless servers plus a cache, and a single well-indexed database with read replicas can often cope. Do the maths out loud. It shows when you don't need sharding.
hint: A day has about 10⁵ seconds.

title: IDs across many shards
prompt: With a sharded database, auto-increment IDs collide across shards. You want IDs that are unique, roughly time-sortable and generated without a central bottleneck. What fits?
choices: Random UUIDv4
Date.now() in milliseconds
One central counter service for every insert
A Snowflake-style ID (timestamp + machine id + sequence) or a UUIDv7
explanation: Snowflake packs a millisecond timestamp, a worker id and a per-millisecond counter into 64 bits: each machine generates IDs independently, and they sort by time. UUIDv7 works the same way in 128 bits. UUIDv4 is unique but random, so inserts land all over the B-tree index, and the IDs don't sort by time. A raw timestamp collides when two inserts share a millisecond. A central counter is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
hint: Combine time, who generated it, and a counter.
